narrativeReportMd:
# EventDefinition R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local EventDefinition element was removed and no existing local cardinality was tightened, so no clear hard R4-instance validation break was found. The meaningful risks are optional R6-only fields, a local primitive type replacement for `usage`, terminology and semantic shifts for subject and jurisdiction metadata, and warning-level canonical constraints.

## Scope
The analysis covered the assigned core resource StructureDefinitions and supporting local terminology artifacts. Inherited Resource/DomainResource content and referenced datatype internals are out of scope except where needed to identify that a change is inherited rather than local.

## Main migration themes
R4-to-R6 migration is mostly shape-compatible for existing instances, but governance metadata semantics are less compatible than the element names suggest. R6 introduces `versionAlgorithm[x]` and `copyrightLabel`, changes `usage` from `string` to `markdown`, changes `subject[x]`'s extensible value set from R4 subject resource types to R6 participant resource types, and redefines `jurisdiction` as the maintaining authority's jurisdiction while encouraging useContext for jurisdictions of use.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact items are not hard cardinality breaks. They are terminology/semantic changes that can alter indexing, selection, and conformance decisions, especially `EventDefinition.jurisdiction` and `EventDefinition.subject[x]`. R6-only `versionAlgorithm[x]` is also important for R6-to-R4 round-tripping because dropping it can change version ordering behavior.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most useful for jurisdiction semantics, subject terminology migration, and deciding whether R6 `versionAlgorithm[x]` can be safely dropped, represented as an extension, or handled by conversion policy.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most R6 changes use optional additions or warning constraints, which preserves R4-to-R6 instance acceptance better than required new fields would have. The less-compatible changes are semantic: the same element names can now imply different governance meaning.

## Follow-up analysis
A separate analysis of shared MetadataResource/CanonicalResource patterns, external terminology.hl7.org jurisdiction content, and primitive datatype changes would improve cross-artifact consistency.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No local removals or cardinality tightening were found for `EventDefinition`. The main migration concerns are R6-only metadata fields, `usage` changing from `string` to `markdown`, and changed subject/jurisdiction conformance semantics. The main uncertainty is terminology behavior without full expansions and official narrative diffs.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should treat EventDefinition as structurally close but semantically updated. R4 instances usually remain representable in R6, but validators and generated models may see changed primitive types, warning constraints, and different terminology bindings. R6-to-R4 conversion needs explicit policy for `versionAlgorithm[x]`, `copyrightLabel`, new subject codes, and jurisdiction/useContext semantics.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for local element presence, cardinality, type, flag, and binding-reference changes because both primary StructureDefinitions were present and parsed. Confidence is medium for terminology impact because expansions and the external R6 jurisdiction ValueSet were not available. Confidence is also limited for prevalence because no corpus of real EventDefinition instances was supplied.

findings.title: R6 adds optional EventDefinition.versionAlgorithm[x]

oldState.summary: No version comparison algorithm element existed on R4 EventDefinition.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could carry a business `version` string but had no local element describing how versions should be ordered.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional `versionAlgorithm[x]` with string and Coding choices.

semanticText.definition: Indicates the mechanism used to compare versions to determine which is more current.
semanticText.comment: If set as a string, this is a FHIRPath expression with %version1 and %version2 context variables.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can explicitly specify version ordering, either with a coded algorithm such as semantic versioning or with a FHIRPath expression.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break because the element is optional and absent from R4 data. It is a round-trip and conversion risk: an R6 EventDefinition that depends on `versionAlgorithm[x]` cannot be represented as a native R4 element, and dropping it can change version selection behavior.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect version ordering can cause the wrong definitional artifact version to be selected, but the direct clinical/business severity depends on downstream use.

justification.inferredGoal: Make version comparison computable instead of relying on opaque business version strings.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `versionAlgorithm[x]` is optional R6 content, not an R4-to-R6 breaking base-design change.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is reasonable: opaque business version strings are not reliably sortable, and R6 adds a standard way to state comparison behavior. Because the element is optional and absent from R4, R4 instances remain acceptable in R6. The compatibility issue is for R6-to-R4 conversion when an R6 instance uses the new element, not for preserving R4-valid instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R6 base alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility. Keeping the algorithm only in an extension would be a downgrade or backport strategy and would make computable version ordering less discoverable to generic R6 systems; it is not a better base-design alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is R6-to-R4 lossiness; an extension is a downgrade mitigation, not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: No matching R4 local element exists.
R6 defines `versionAlgorithm[x]` as 0..1 with `string` and `Coding` choices.
evidence.quote: Indicates the mechanism used to compare versions to determine which is more current.

evidence.detail: The R6 value set includes the version-algorithm CodeSystem.

examples.examplesMd: The example is illustrative and focuses on the R6-only element; a complete valid EventDefinition may require additional context.

findings.narrativeMd: `EventDefinition.versionAlgorithm[x]` is a new R6 metadata element. It does not break existing R4 instances, but it gives R6 instances version-ordering semantics that R4 has no native place to store.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is unaffected when the element is absent. R6-to-R4 conversion is lossy unless a cross-version extension or side-channel is used. Strict R4 parsers will reject an R6 JSON instance containing `versionAlgorithmString` or `versionAlgorithmCoding` as an unknown element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When converting R6 to R4, preserve the algorithm in an agreed extension if version ordering matters. Test conversion using semantic versioning, date-like versions, and opaque strings. If the element is dropped, document that version ordering reverts to implementation-specific behavior.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The optional addition was relatively backward-compatible for R4-to-R6. The unavoidable incompatibility is that R4's base model cannot carry the information without an extension.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is recommended when an R6 artifact includes a FHIRPath string algorithm because safe downgrade may require evaluating or preserving executable logic.

findings.title: R6 adds optional EventDefinition.copyrightLabel

oldState.summary: R4 had only `EventDefinition.copyright` for copyright and restriction text.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 did not distinguish a short renderable copyright label from the broader copyright or license statement.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional `copyrightLabel` as a short string for rendering.

semanticText.definition: A short string (<50 characters), suitable for inclusion in a page footer that identifies the copyright holder, effective period, and optionally whether rights are restricted.
semanticText.comment: The copyright symbol and the '(c)' textual representation SHOULD NOT be included in this string.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 separates a compact display label from the full `copyright` statement.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The element is optional, so R4 instances remain structurally acceptable in R6. R6 instances that populate it are not directly representable in R4 without an extension or a lossy merge into `copyright`.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily legal/display metadata loss rather than clinical safety.

justification.inferredGoal: Support consistent short copyright rendering while keeping full legal text in `copyright`.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `copyrightLabel` is an optional additive R6 element and does not invalidate R4 EventDefinition instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of separating a short renderable copyright label from full copyright or licensing text is clear and low risk. The base change is optional, so it preserves R4-to-R6 instance compatibility while improving R6 rendering consistency.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A standard extension could carry this value in R4 or during downgrade, but that is a conversion/backport mitigation. In the R6 base model, an optional element is already compatibility-preserving for R4-to-R6 migration and gives generic renderers a visible place for the label.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The main cost is R6-to-R4 downgrade lossiness; an extension can mitigate downgrade but is not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: No R4 local element exists.
R6 defines `copyrightLabel` as 0..1 string.
evidence.quote: A short string (<50 characters), suitable for inclusion in a page footer...

examples.examplesMd: Merging the label into `copyright` is lossy because R4 cannot distinguish a display label from full legal text.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds `copyrightLabel` for short rendered copyright information. This is non-breaking for R4-to-R6 but creates a downgrade decision for R6 artifacts.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance without the field remains acceptable in R6. A strict R4 parser will reject an R6 instance containing `copyrightLabel` unless the element is removed or converted to an extension.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, either preserve `copyrightLabel` in an extension or concatenate it into `copyright` with a clear convention. Legal or publishing workflows should test that rendered notices are not lost.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: An optional element is less disruptive than changing `copyright` cardinality or type. R4 compatibility could only have been preserved by using an extension, which would reduce generic R6 renderer support.

findings.title: EventDefinition.usage changes primitive type from string to markdown

semanticText.short: Describes the clinical usage of the event definition
semanticText.definition: A detailed description of how the event definition is used from a clinical perspective.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled usage guidance as a plain FHIR string.

semanticText.short: Describes the clinical usage of the event definition
semanticText.definition: A detailed description of how the event definition is used from a clinical perspective.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 treats usage guidance as markdown, aligning it with other narrative metadata fields.

facts.note: The wire representation remains a string, but FHIR type identity and generated models change.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Most JSON values that were valid R4 strings should still be lexically acceptable as markdown, so this is not a clear data-shape break. However, generated APIs, primitive wrapper classes, XML/JSON schema validation, and FHIRPath type checks may distinguish `string` from `markdown`.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The field is descriptive guidance; the primary risk is rendering or code compatibility rather than direct patient safety.

justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `usage` as `string` with markdown guidance, or add a parallel optional markdown-specific element.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal, allowing formatted clinical usage guidance, is reasonable. Most wire-level R4 string values remain string-shaped in R6 markdown, but generated models and strict type-aware tooling can still break because the primitive identity changed. Given the value of explicit markdown semantics and the tradeoffs of the less-breaking options, the type replacement is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could have retained `usage` as `string` and documented that markdown syntax may appear, preserving generated R4-style APIs. That would not reliably tell generic R6 renderers to treat the content as markdown. A new `usageMarkdown` field would preserve the old field but create duplicate representations for the same guidance and require rules for which field is authoritative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping `string` weakens computable markdown/rendering semantics; a parallel field duplicates content and needs precedence rules.

evidence.detail: R4 declares `usage` as type `string`.
R6 declares `usage` as type `markdown`.
Both primitives serialize through string values in the supplied packages, but they remain distinct FHIR primitive types.

oldValidNewInvalidJson.usage: Use when a named event occurs.

examples.examplesMd: The example is not expected to become invalid on the JSON wire; it illustrates an R4 instance whose generated property type changes from string to markdown in R6.

findings.narrativeMd: `usage` keeps the same cardinality and JSON scalar shape but changes FHIR primitive identity. This matters most for code generators and strict validators that expose or enforce primitive types.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A plain R4 JSON string should generally remain acceptable as R6 markdown, so hard instance breakage is only potential. Runtime breakage is more plausible: generated model properties, serializers, and FHIRPath expressions that expected `string` may need to handle `markdown`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review generated EventDefinition models and mapping code for `usage`. Treat existing text as markdown-safe plain text unless it contains characters that a renderer interprets unexpectedly. Add tests for plain text, markdown formatting, and extensions on the primitive element.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A less disruptive alternative would have left the primitive type as `string` and documented markdown allowance, but that would weaken semantic precision. A new optional field would avoid type replacement but introduce duplication.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The hard-instance impact depends on validator behavior for markdown primitives and is therefore marked Potential rather than Yes.

findings.title: EventDefinition.subject[x] CodeableConcept binding changes from subject-type to participant-resource-types

oldState.summary: R4 used an extensible binding to `ValueSet/subject-type`.

binding.description: The possible types of subjects for an event (E.g. Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Location, etc.).

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R4 compose explicitly includes five codes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/resource-types`.

semanticText.definition: A code or group definition that describes the intended subject of the event definition.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed a CodeableConcept subject using selected resource type codes from the R4 `resource-types` system, or a Reference to Group.

newState.summary: R6 uses an extensible binding to `ValueSet/participant-resource-types`.

binding.description: The possible types of subjects for an event (E.g. Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Location, etc.).

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The R6 compose explicitly includes ten participant resource type codes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-types`, including the five R4 concepts by code name but under a different system URI.

semanticText.definition: A code or group definition that describes the intended subject of the event definition.

newState.narrativeMd: The choice types and Group reference target remain the same, but the CodeableConcept value set changes to a broader participant-oriented set and a different code system.

facts.oldValue: http://hl7.org/fhir/resource-types: Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Location, Device

facts.newValue: http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-types: CareTeam, Device, Group, HealthcareService, Location, Organization, Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson

facts.note: No Reference target change was found.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Because the binding is extensible, the value-set change is not a direct required-code validation break. It can still affect validators, authoring tools, generated terminology enums, and selection logic. R6 also permits participant codes such as `CareTeam`, `PractitionerRole`, and `RelatedPerson` that are outside the R4 subject-type value set.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Subject type drives applicability of an event definition. Misclassifying the target population or participant type can lead to inappropriate triggering or filtering.

justification.inferredGoal: Align subject metadata with a broader participant resource type vocabulary.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Use a transitional base value set that includes both R4 `resource-types` subject codes and R6 `fhir-types` participant codes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of aligning subject metadata with a broader participant-resource vocabulary is reasonable. A less-breaking value-set design could have accepted the old resource-type codings while adding the new participant codes, but that would leave two code systems for overlapping resource concepts and complicate validation, indexing, and ConceptMap policy. Those material terminology tradeoffs make the R6 binding change probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best base alternative would be a transitional value set containing both `http://hl7.org/fhir/resource-types#Patient`-style R4 codings and `http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-types#Patient`-style R6 codings, plus the new participant resource types. This would preserve more R4 terminology conformance, but it risks indefinite dual coding for the same fact and inconsistent authoring choices across implementations.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves old codings but creates duplicate same-resource representations and terminology ambiguity that may persist indefinitely.

evidence.detail: R4 binds subject[x] to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/subject-type` with extensible strength.
R6 binds subject[x] to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/participant-resource-types` with extensible strength.
R4 subject-type includes Patient, Practitioner, Organization, Location, and Device from `http://hl7.org/fhir/resource-types`.
R6 participant-resource-types includes ten codes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-types`.

examples.examplesMd: Dual-coding may be useful during transition, but profiles should state which coding is authoritative.

findings.narrativeMd: `subject[x]` did not change shape, but its CodeableConcept binding changed substantially. The binding is extensible, so this is not a simple invalidation, but terminology-aware systems will see a different value set and code system.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances using `http://hl7.org/fhir/resource-types#Patient` may no longer satisfy the R6 value set without translation to `http://hl7.org/fhir/fhir-types#Patient`. Conversely, R6 subjects such as `PractitionerRole` or `CareTeam` do not fit the R4 subject-type value set. Validator behavior depends on extensible binding policy.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define a ConceptMap or deterministic mapping from R4 resource-type codings to R6 fhir-type codings for overlapping codes. For R6-only participant codes, decide whether to preserve them as extensions, downgrade to a broader supported code, or require manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The model preserved the element and choice types, which is good for wire compatibility. The main avoidable pain would have been reduced by publishing explicit cross-version terminology mappings and perhaps broadening the old value set instead of switching canonical value sets.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Terminology expansions were not available; the code comparison is based on ValueSet compose definitions in the supplied packages.

findings.title: EventDefinition.jurisdiction changes from intended jurisdiction of use to maintaining authority jurisdiction

oldState.summary: R4 `jurisdiction` described where the EventDefinition was intended to be used.

binding.description: Countries and regions within which this artifact is targeted for use.

semanticText.short: Intended jurisdiction for event definition (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the event definition is intended to be used.
semanticText.comment: It may be possible for the event definition to be used in jurisdictions other than those for which it was originally designed or intended.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 consumers could reasonably use `jurisdiction` as an applicability or intended-use jurisdiction.

newState.summary: R6 `jurisdiction` describes the jurisdiction of the authority maintaining the EventDefinition, and recommends useContext for jurisdictions of use.

binding.description: Countries and regions within which this artifact is targeted for use.

semanticText.short: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the event definition (if applicable)
semanticText.definition: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating. In general, the jurisdiction is also found in the useContext. The useContext may reference additional jurisdictions because the defining jurisdiction does not necessarily limit the jurisdictions of use.
semanticText.comment: DEPRECATION NOTE: implementations are encouraged to migrate to using the new 'jurisdiction' code in the useContext element.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 narrows the meaning of the element to maintaining authority jurisdiction and moves intended-use jurisdiction guidance toward `useContext`.

facts.oldValue: Intended jurisdiction for event definition (if applicable)
facts.newValue: Jurisdiction of the authority that maintains the event definition (if applicable)

facts.oldValue: A legal or geographic region in which the event definition is intended to be used.
facts.newValue: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating.
DEPRECATION NOTE recommends useContext.code jurisdiction for intended-use jurisdiction.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The cardinality and datatype did not change, so data remains structurally valid. The same field now answers a different governance question. Systems that filter EventDefinitions by intended jurisdiction may return different results if they keep reading R6 `jurisdiction` as R4 intended-use metadata.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Jurisdiction can drive local policy, clinical content selection, and legal applicability. Misinterpreting maintaining-authority jurisdiction as intended-use jurisdiction can select inappropriate content.

justification.inferredGoal: Distinguish publisher/maintainer jurisdiction from jurisdictions where the artifact may be used.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve `jurisdiction` as intended-use jurisdiction and add optional maintainer or authority jurisdiction metadata for the new fact.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of distinguishing the maintaining authority's jurisdiction from jurisdictions of use is reasonable. However, redefining the existing `jurisdiction` element changes the meaning of R4 data without a shape or validation signal. A straightforward additive design could meet the same goal while preserving the R4 meaning of existing instances, so this level of semantic breakage was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking R6 base design would leave `jurisdiction` as the intended-use jurisdiction and add an optional element, or a clearly named canonical-resource metadata slot, for maintaining-authority jurisdiction. Implementations could still use `useContext` for additional applicability jurisdictions. The cost is extra model surface and less uniformity with any broader canonical-resource cleanup, but those tradeoffs are moderate compared with silently changing existing business-rule semantics.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Adds another governance metadata slot and may reduce cross-canonical uniformity, but avoids silent reinterpretation of existing data.

evidence.detail: R4 defines jurisdiction as the region where the event definition is intended to be used.
evidence.quote: A legal or geographic region in which the event definition is intended to be used.

evidence.detail: R6 defines jurisdiction as the region of the maintaining authority and adds a deprecation note recommending `useContext` for jurisdiction of use.
evidence.quote: A legal or geographic region in which the authority that maintains the resource is operating.

evidence.detail: The binding canonical changes from `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/jurisdiction` to `http://terminology.hl7.org/ValueSet/jurisdiction`.

examples.examplesMd: The old-valid example is not structurally invalid in R6; it is semantically risky if `US` meant intended use rather than maintaining authority.

findings.narrativeMd: `jurisdiction` is one of the most important semantic changes. The element remains in place, but its meaning shifts from intended jurisdiction of use to jurisdiction of the maintaining authority, with intended use moving toward `useContext`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Strict instance validation is unlikely to fail solely because of this change. Compatibility risk is semantic: existing R4 data can be read differently by R6 business rules. R6 data using `useContext` with a jurisdiction code may also lose intended-use semantics when downgraded to R4 unless conversion policy maps it carefully.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit uses of `jurisdiction` in repositories, search indexes, and selection rules. If an R4 value represented intended use, populate an R6 `useContext` jurisdiction as well as, or instead of, `jurisdiction` according to local policy. Do not assume a lossless R6-to-R4 conversion without deciding how to merge maintaining-authority and intended-use jurisdictions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This semantic reuse was probably avoidable by adding a new maintainer-jurisdiction element, but the R6 pattern may be part of a broader canonical resource governance cleanup. Human review is needed because the computable diff does not provide rationale.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 external jurisdiction ValueSet was not available locally, so binding-content impact is less certain than the semantic text change.

findings.title: EventDefinition.experimental has stronger R6 lifecycle meaning

oldState.summary: R4 `experimental` indicated the current event definition was for testing, education, evaluation, or marketing and not intended for genuine usage.

semanticText.short: For testing purposes, not real usage
semanticText.definition: A Boolean value to indicate that this event definition is authored for testing purposes (or education/evaluation/marketing) and is not intended to be used for genuine usage.
semanticText.comment: Allows filtering of event definitions that are appropriate for use versus not.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 described experimental status mostly as a current-use filter.

newState.summary: R6 says no version of an experimental resource will ever be intended for genuine usage and defines missing as not experimental.

semanticText.short: For testing only - never for real usage
semanticText.definition: A Boolean value to indicate that this event definition is authored for testing purposes (or education/evaluation/marketing) and no version of this resource will ever be intended for genuine usage.
semanticText.comment: If experimental is 'true' for any version of a resource, it should be true for all versions of the resource.
semanticText.meaningWhenMissing: If absent, this resource is treated as though it is not experimental.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 makes the flag a stronger lifecycle assertion across all versions, not merely a current testing marker.

facts.oldValue: For testing purposes, not real usage
facts.newValue: For testing only - never for real usage

facts.oldValue: not intended to be used for genuine usage
facts.newValue: no version of this resource will ever be intended for genuine usage
If absent, this resource is treated as though it is not experimental.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The boolean shape and cardinality are unchanged, but an R4 artifact marked experimental for a temporary testing phase may carry a stronger R6 implication that all versions are never for real use. Filtering and publication workflows can therefore change behavior without a validation error.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrectly treating production-intended content as permanently experimental, or vice versa, can affect artifact availability in clinical decision support deployments.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that experimental artifacts are never production-intended and may change without version guarantees.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the old current-use `experimental` meaning and add a separate never-production lifecycle qualifier, or make the stronger rule best-practice guidance.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of making experimental content clearly non-production and unstable is reasonable for safety and publication governance. The change does not alter the element shape, but it can surprise R4 workflows that treated `experimental=true` as temporary. Less-breaking approaches exist, yet they either split lifecycle meaning across multiple flags or weaken consistent interpretation, so the semantic tightening is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could preserve the R4 meaning and add a new optional qualifier for resources that will never be production-intended, or state the cross-version rule as best-practice guidance. That would protect workflows where experimental content later graduates, but it increases lifecycle metadata complexity and risks inconsistent filtering if systems only inspect one flag.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Separate lifecycle flags complicate filtering and authoring; guidance-only may not deliver uniform safety semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 defines experimental as authored for testing/education/evaluation/marketing and not intended for genuine usage.
R6 says no version will ever be intended for genuine usage and adds meaningWhenMissing.
evidence.quote: If experimental is 'true' for any version of a resource, it should be true for all versions of the resource.

examples.examplesMd: The example remains structurally valid in R6; the compatibility issue is lifecycle interpretation if the artifact was expected to become production-intended later.

findings.narrativeMd: `experimental` is structurally unchanged but semantically stronger in R6. Migration tools should not treat this as a no-op when artifact lifecycle state drives publication or deployment.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No old-valid instance becomes invalid solely because of this text change. Runtime systems that filter on `experimental` may behave differently because R6 defines absence as false and true as a cross-version never-production assertion.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review artifacts with `experimental=true`. If the artifact was merely a draft on a path to production, consider whether it should remain the same canonical resource in R6 or be reissued with corrected lifecycle metadata.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been less surprising as supplemental guidance, but clarifying the existing flag avoids creating another lifecycle element.

findings.title: EventDefinition.date changes from publication date wording to last significant change wording

oldState.summary: R4 described `date` as when the event definition was published.

semanticText.definition: The date (and optionally time) when the event definition was published.
semanticText.comment: The date is not the same as the resource last-modified-date.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 tied the field definition to publication timing while also saying it changes with substantive content, version, or status changes.

newState.summary: R6 describes `date` as when the event definition was last significantly changed.

semanticText.definition: The date (and optionally time) when the event definition was last significantly changed.
semanticText.comment: The date is often not tracked until the resource is published, but may be present on draft content.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 aligns the definition with change tracking and explicitly allows draft content to carry the date.

facts.oldValue: when the event definition was published
facts.newValue: when the event definition was last significantly changed
The date is often not tracked until the resource is published, but may be present on draft content.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The datatype and cardinality are unchanged, but systems that use `date` as a publication date may need to revisit sorting, freshness, and release-date logic. Downgrading R6 to R4 can also relabel a last-change date as a publication date.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is generally governance and artifact freshness rather than direct clinical safety.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify the date's role as a significant-change/revision date.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `date` as publication date and add explicit publication-date and last-significant-change date separation.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is to resolve ambiguity around what `date` represents. R4 already had the short label `Date last changed` and required the date to change with version, status, or substantive content, so R6 appears to clarify an inconsistent definition rather than introduce a wholly new concept. A separate-field design would be less disruptive for systems that used the field strictly as a publication date, but the added complexity makes the R6 clarification probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking design could leave `date` as publication date and add a new last-significant-change element, or add both explicit publication and revision dates. That would preserve publication-date consumers but create overlapping date fields and require migration policy for legacy values whose R4 meaning was already ambiguous.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Clearer for publication workflows but adds overlapping date metadata and migration rules; R4 text already mixed publication and change-date semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 definition says `date` is when the event definition was published.
R6 definition says `date` is when the event definition was last significantly changed.

examples.examplesMd: A date value such as `2024-01-15` remains syntactically valid; the migration issue is whether it is interpreted as publication date or revision date.

findings.narrativeMd: `date` is a semantic compatibility issue rather than a structural one. R6 makes the field a last-significant-change date, while R4 wording emphasized publication.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No validation break is expected. Business rules that sort by publication date, calculate artifact age, or determine latest content may change behavior if they do not distinguish publication and revision semantics.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit uses of `EventDefinition.date` in repositories and publication tooling. If a separate publication date is needed, preserve it through Provenance, extensions, or release metadata rather than assuming `date` carries that meaning in R6.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change likely fixes a pre-existing ambiguity. A more backward-compatible but larger change would have introduced explicit separate date fields.

findings.title: R6 strengthens warning-level canonical name and URL constraints

oldState.summary: R4 had warning invariant `evd-0` for machine-friendly names and no local URL warning on EventDefinition.url.

constraints.human: Name should be usable as an identifier for the module by machine processing applications such as code generation

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 warned that `name` should be code-generation friendly, allowing a single initial capital letter by regex.

newState.summary: R6 replaces the name warning with `cnl-0` and adds URL warning `cnl-1` prohibiting `|`, `#`, and spaces.

constraints.human: Name should be usable as an identifier for the module by machine processing applications such as code generation
URL should not contain | or # - these characters make processing canonical references problematic

newState.narrativeMd: R6 canonical-resource warning rules are more explicit and include a new URL hygiene warning.

facts.note: These are warning-level constraints, not error-level invariants.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The constraints are warnings, so ordinary validation should not reject instances solely for these conditions. They can still affect CI pipelines, publication tooling, and code generation policies that fail on warnings.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily broken canonical reference parsing or generated code names, not direct clinical safety.

justification.inferredGoal: Prevent canonical reference parsing problems and improve machine-friendly artifact names.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: warning-level constraints do not make R4 instances invalid in the R6 base model.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of improving canonical URL and machine-name hygiene is reasonable, and R6 used warning severity rather than error severity. That preserves base instance validity while still surfacing interoperability risks around canonical parsing and code generation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking alternative assessment applies because the R6 design is already warning-only for base validation. A purely narrative note would be less disruptive for warning-failing CI pipelines, but it would not provide equivalent computable guidance; making the rules errors would have been the genuinely breaking design.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Systems that fail on warnings may need policy changes; a narrative-only note would be less visible to validators.

evidence.detail: R4 root warning checks name format with `evd-0`.
R6 root warning uses `cnl-0` with an anchored name regex.
R6 adds a warning that URL should not contain `|`, `#`, or spaces.

examples.examplesMd: The example would be expected to produce R6 warnings, not R6 errors, because both changed constraints have warning severity.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 makes canonical artifact hygiene more visible by warning on problematic URLs and tightening the recommended machine-name regex. This mostly affects validation pipelines and publication QA.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with a URL containing `#`, `|`, or a space, or a one-character name such as `A`, can become warning-nonconformant in R6. It should not become invalid unless a local validator treats warnings as failures.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review canonical URLs and machine names before publication. Avoid embedding version separators or fragments in `url`; use canonical version syntax and separate `version` instead. Decide whether CI treats warning constraints as blocking.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Warning severity is the compatibility-preserving design. The same guidance as an error would have been a hard break.

findings.title: R6 governance text narrows publisher and copyright interpretation

oldState.summary: R4 publisher named the organization or individual that published the event definition; copyright was framed as use/publishing restrictions.

semanticText.short: Name of the publisher (organization or individual)
semanticText.definition: The name of the organization or individual that published the event definition.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 governance text focused on publication and legal restrictions.

newState.summary: R6 publisher names the party responsible for release and ongoing maintenance; copyright is framed as intellectual-property notice and points short labels to `copyrightLabel`.

semanticText.short: Name of the publisher/steward (organization or individual)
semanticText.definition: The name of the organization or individual responsible for the release and ongoing maintenance of the event definition.
semanticText.comment: Short copyright declaration should be sent in `copyrightLabel`.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 governance text emphasizes stewardship and separates full copyright notice from short display label.

facts.oldValue: Name of the publisher (organization or individual)
facts.newValue: Name of the publisher/steward (organization or individual)
responsible for the release and ongoing maintenance of the event definition

facts.oldValue: Copyright statements are generally legal restrictions on the use and publishing of the event definition.
facts.newValue: Copyright statements are notices of intellectual property ownership and can include restrictions on the use and publishing of the event definition.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The fields remain optional with the same primitive types, but governance workflows may interpret the values differently. R4 data that recorded a one-time publisher may not identify the R6 steward responsible for ongoing maintenance.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is mainly attribution, maintenance contact, and rights-display accuracy.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify governance responsibility and separate full copyright notice from short display label.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve publisher as publisher-of-record and add optional steward or maintenance-responsibility metadata while keeping copyright label separate.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of clarifying stewardship and copyright display responsibilities is reasonable. The publisher change is partly a clarification because the R4 comment already described the publisher or steward as responsible for maintenance, and the copyright label is an optional additive element. A less-breaking design exists for publisher semantics, but it would add more governance fields and role distinctions, so the R6 approach is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could keep `publisher` defined as the publisher of record, add a separate optional steward or maintainer element, and rely on `copyrightLabel` only for display labels. That would make migration intent clearer but would increase model surface and create a long-term need to distinguish publisher, steward, maintainer, and contact responsibilities across canonical resources.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids semantic drift but expands governance metadata and may duplicate closely related publisher/steward roles.

evidence.detail: R4 publisher definition says the organization or individual published the event definition.
R6 publisher definition says responsible for release and ongoing maintenance.
R6 directs short copyright declarations to `copyrightLabel`.

examples.examplesMd: A value such as `publisher: Example Hospital` remains valid, but migration may need to confirm whether the organization is merely the publisher of record or the ongoing steward.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 governance wording changes are low-level but relevant for repositories that use EventDefinition metadata to assign stewardship, contact responsibility, or copyright rendering.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No structural validation break is expected. The compatibility issue is that the same `publisher` string may answer a different operational question in R6.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review publisher/steward metadata for managed EventDefinition catalogs. If the R4 publisher is not the ongoing steward, update R6 publisher/contact metadata or record the distinction in extensions or Provenance.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The wording change preserves wire compatibility but not necessarily governance semantics. A less ambiguous alternative would have added a separate steward field.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The R6 StructureDefinition exists at the expected path and keeps the same canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, abstract flag, and `DomainResource` baseDefinition. Maturity/status changed but no rename, split, merge, or removal was found.

No local R4 EventDefinition element was removed. The only local additions found were optional R6 elements `versionAlgorithm[x]` and `copyrightLabel`, both reported as findings because of R6-to-R4 representability risk.
All common local elements kept the same min/max cardinality, including required `status` (1..1) and required repeating `trigger` (1..*).
`EventDefinition.subject[x]` remains a choice of `CodeableConcept` or `Reference(Group)`. No local reference target additions, removals, or replacements were found.
`EventDefinition.status` remains a modifier element with the same modifier reason. No local modifier flag changes were found.
Local `isSummary` flags were materially stable. R6 explicitly includes `mustSupport: false` where R4 omitted it; this was treated as an explicit false default rather than a behavior change.
No local slicing changes were found in EventDefinition.
No local fixed value, pattern, or default value constraints were found to change.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex value-limit changes were found on EventDefinition elements beyond datatype-level primitive definitions, which are out of scope.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds deprecation guidance encouraging topic metadata in useContext
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `topic` remains present with the same 0..* cardinality, CodeableConcept type, and example binding canonical. Existing R4 instances remain structurally representable.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: For R6 authoring, consider adding `useContext` with `usage-context-type#topic` while preserving `topic` as required by local profiles or search behavior.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: PublicationStatus required binding version changes but codes remain the same
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Both R4 and R6 bind `status` with required strength to publication-status, and the supplied CodeSystems contain the same codes: `draft`, `active`, `retired`, and `unknown`.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Generated terminology bindings may point at version-specific canonical URLs (`|4.0.1` vs `|6.0.0-ballot4`), but no code migration was identified.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: StructureDefinition status/maturity changes from draft/trial-use to active/normative
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This changes specification maturity metadata, not the instance shape of EventDefinition.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Implementers may treat R6 EventDefinition as more stable and may update conformance documentation accordingly.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Description comment no longer lists 'why the event definition was built' as an example
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The element type, cardinality, and core definition are unchanged; the edit appears to clarify examples rather than prohibit content.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: No transform is needed. If systems separated rationale from description, continue using `purpose` for why the artifact exists.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Several local EventDefinition changes appear to reflect broader canonical resource governance patterns. A shared interface-level analysis should de-duplicate cross-artifact migration guidance.
The R6 jurisdiction binding references an external ValueSet not present in the local R6 core package. Expansion and compose comparison would improve terminology confidence.
`EventDefinition.usage` changes from `string` to `markdown`; datatype-level lexical and codegen implications should be assessed in the primitive datatype report.
Inherited DomainResource constraints and inherited elements were intentionally excluded from EventDefinition findings under the base-artifact scope rule.
